motion: Are apostolic martyrdom and suffering good evidence for the resurrection?

bridges.description: Whether costly apostolic conduct supports sincere claimed experiences as one contribution to a larger resurrection case.
Whether early varied sources extend appearance belief beyond Peter and Paul to the apostolic group.
Whether public proclamation amid danger supports sincerity without proving every death tradition.
Whether the strongest individual death traditions strengthen the sincerity case.
Whether sincere suffering by a limited number leaves a gap between belief and resurrection truth.
Whether sources establish firsthand claims for the group rather than chiefly Peter and Paul.
Whether evidence connects particular deaths to resurrection proclamation.
Whether sincere error and ordinary motivations explain the accepted cases.

sections.title: Definition and evidential role
sections.rationale: Fixes what martyrdom evidence would need to show and whether its function is death, sincerity, or a broader conclusion.

sections.title: Eyewitness scope and source reliability
sections.rationale: Addresses how many firsthand witnesses are supported and whether group references justify extension beyond named figures.

sections.title: Death evidence and individual cases
sections.rationale: Assesses the strength and limits of individual death traditions directly required by the motion.

sections.title: Sincere error and alternative explanations
sections.rationale: Tests whether accepted sincerity closes the gap to resurrection or permits ordinary explanations.

sections.title: Historical standards and checkability
sections.rationale: The speakers directly dispute whether living-witness claims were practically testable and whether the historical standard is overly skeptical.

sections.title: Final motion-level synthesis
sections.rationale: Preserves each side’s qualified independent conclusion.

moves.speaker: Paulogia
moves.claim: Paulogia clearly requires a claimed resurrection eyewitness, a chance to recant, and an actual death-level test rather than mere willingness to suffer or die.
moves.warrant: He explains that the familiar argument about dying for a known lie has force only when the person was positioned to know and the historical case connects that knowledge to the cost imposed.
moves.inference: Broad willingness to suffer or die has less evidential force when eyewitness status, recantation opportunity, or actual death is not established.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This speaker-owned passage contains Paulogia’s proposed criteria and explanation of why eyewitness status and a death-level test matter, ending before the moderator recap.
moves.attributionRationale: The speaker and the eyewitness, recantation, and actual-death contrast are clear, but one clause in the third criterion is materially uncertain.
moves.audioVerificationReason: Verify the uncertain third-criterion wording, including whether chose not to die was spoken as captioned or was a spoken slip; do not use that clause independently or penalize its coherence.
moves.importanceRationale: This sets con’s test for when martyrdom contacts the motion.

burdenContact.rationale: It specifies the required connection among firsthand knowledge, recantation, and death.

moves.speaker: Sean McDowell
moves.claim: Martyrdom need not require a recorded recantation opportunity when someone publicly persists in a dangerous religious message and is killed in connection with it.
moves.warrant: McDowell appeals to martyrdom scholarship and a modern priest widely called a martyr despite no recorded recantation offer.
moves.inference: Paulogia’s recantation criteria are more restrictive than the category needed to assess apostolic suffering.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The passage preserves the scholarly definition, illustration, and conclusion against the proposed criteria.
moves.attributionRationale: McDowell directly addresses Paulogia and sustains the same response.
moves.importanceRationale: The definition controls which cases can enter the pro argument.

burdenContact.rationale: It makes costly public proclamation relevant without a recorded recantation scene.

responseComponents.description: Challenges the necessity of an explicit recantation opportunity by offering a broader costly-public-proclamation definition.

moves.speaker: Paulogia
moves.claim: Even granting McDowell’s broader definition would not show that the apostles meet it.
moves.warrant: The sources often do not show what particular apostles preached, why they died, or whether politics rather than resurrection proclamation caused a death.
moves.inference: A permissive definition cannot replace case-specific historical evidence.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This complete reply begins with the conditional grant and ends with the political-versus-ideological objection.
moves.attributionRationale: The explicit pushback and sustained first-person objections identify Paulogia.
moves.importanceRationale: It separates a definition from the factual burden.

burdenContact.rationale: It insists on evidence connecting each death to the relevant proclamation.

responseComponents.description: Grants the broader definition for argument and disputes that the cited apostolic cases satisfy its factual requirements.

moves.speaker: Sean McDowell
moves.claim: Apostolic suffering and death do not prove resurrection or Christianity; they contribute by supporting sincere belief and countering invention or conspiracy.
moves.warrant: McDowell expressly places the fate argument as one premise within a larger resurrection case.
moves.inference: The evidence can be relevant even if it establishes only sincerity rather than resurrection itself.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This compact passage contains the express limitation, positive role, and anti-conspiracy implication.
moves.attributionRationale: The first-person limitation is explicit.
moves.importanceRationale: This defines the actual affirmative burden.

burdenContact.rationale: It states how suffering is offered as resurrection evidence.

moves.speaker: Paulogia
moves.claim: The evidential force changes sharply if reliable firsthand belief is limited to a handful, perhaps chiefly Peter and Paul.
moves.warrant: A small number of sincere people can be wrong without requiring a collective-experience explanation.
moves.inference: The scope of demonstrated eyewitness belief is load-bearing for the motion.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The passage preserves Paulogia’s sincerity concession, dispute over the group term, and explanatory consequence.
moves.attributionRationale: Paulogia’s concession and numerical contrast are clear without relying on an exact count.
moves.importanceRationale: This is the central restriction on group extension.

burdenContact.rationale: It makes the supported number of firsthand claimants central.

responseComponents.description: Accepts the limited sincerity role but argues its force depends on how many firsthand claimants are established.

moves.speaker: Sean McDowell
moves.claim: History need not require each apostle’s own writing because early sources of different genres consistently report appearances to the apostles and named figures.
moves.warrant: McDowell invokes Acts, Luke, Paul, early church testimony, and the earliest resurrection proclamation.
moves.inference: The basis for group appearance belief extends beyond explicit first-person statements by Peter and Paul.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The response begins with the methodological answer and ends with the group-sincerity implication.
moves.attributionRationale: The methodological argument is clear; garbled names and dates are not material.
moves.importanceRationale: This is the main pro answer to the narrow eyewitness pool.

burdenContact.rationale: It explains why collective and indirect early testimony can support the group claim.

responseComponents.description: Rejects the premise that historical knowledge requires each witness’s own surviving first-person statement.

moves.speaker: Paulogia
moves.claim: Acts material about the early apostles is indirect rather than firsthand and should be treated as a claim requiring source evaluation.
moves.warrant: Even if Luke accompanied Paul, the relevant chapters precede Paul’s conversion and depend on unidentified earlier reports.
moves.inference: Acts does not independently establish that each apostle personally claimed an appearance.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The span contains the source-status objection and its chain-of-transmission reason, stopping before captions overlap the frozen break boundary.
moves.attributionRationale: The source criticism and speaker are explicit.
moves.importanceRationale: This contests a central source for broadening the group.

burdenContact.rationale: It challenges whether Acts supplies firsthand evidence.

responseComponents.description: Challenges the firsthand and independent status of Acts as evidence for the wider group.

moves.speaker: Sean McDowell
moves.claim: Acts has historical standing, and early multiply attested appearance claims support that disciples believed they experienced the risen Jesus.
moves.warrant: McDowell points to correspondence with known history and the early First Corinthians 15 creed naming individuals and groups.
moves.inference: The group belief is historically usable without treating every narrative detail as true.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: After the excluded break, this response develops Acts, the early creed, multiple attestation, and closes with the limited sincerity inference.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: the disciples all believed they had seen the Risen Jesus
moves.attributionRationale: The overall argument is clear, but scholar names, a percentage, and creed wording are garbled.
moves.audioVerificationReason: Verify named authorities, numerical consensus, and exact creed wording if materially relied upon.
moves.importanceRationale: This is the main affirmative evidence for group belief.

burdenContact.rationale: It combines source reliability, an early creed, and multiple attestation.

responseComponents.description: Answers the source-chain objection with Acts, an early creed, and multiple attestation while retaining a limited sincerity inference.

moves.speaker: Paulogia
moves.claim: Paulogia argues that Acts may depend on Josephus, does not align well with Paul’s missions, and that broad survey agreement about disciples can be driven by well-attested figures while masking disagreement about most named apostles.
moves.warrant: He says occasional Josephus agreement is unsurprising if Josephus was a source, disputes correspondence between Acts and Pauline letters, and contrasts strong Peter-Paul attestation with uncertainty when the remaining apostles are listed individually.
moves.inference: Neither source overlap nor grouped scholarly language by itself establishes independent firsthand resurrection belief for every apostle later used in the suffering argument.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This full Paulogia reply preserves the distinct Josephus-dependence criticism, Acts-Paul mismatch, and survey-aggregation objection through the moderator handoff.
moves.attributionRationale: Paulogia’s direct discussion of the survey and named individuals clearly owns the passage.
moves.importanceRationale: It combines two independently relevant limits on the group inference: source dependence and aggregation across uneven individual evidence.

burdenContact.rationale: It tests whether collective survey wording supports each apostle.

responseComponents.description: Challenges both the claimed independence of Acts-related corroboration and the move from broad scholarly agreement about disciples to comparable evidence for each named apostle.

moves.audioVerificationReason: Verify material details of the Bulls analogy before adjudication; the collective-reference inference is clear.
moves.speaker: Sean McDowell
moves.claim: Ordinary historical language can identify a known group without naming every member.
moves.warrant: McDowell uses an announcer referring to the Bulls as a team and applies the same collective-reference logic to early references to the apostles.
moves.inference: Silence about individual names in a given source does not reduce the group evidence to only one named person and unknown others.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: After the moderator’s recap, McDowell’s speaker-owned answer contains the full group-reference analogy and applies it to the apostles before Paulogia replies.
moves.attributionRationale: The collective-reference reasoning is clear, but several player names and phrases in the analogy are garbled.
moves.importanceRationale: It is a distinct methodological answer to the individual-name objection.

burdenContact.rationale: It defends collective references as evidence about a recognized group.

responseComponents.description: Answers the premise that lack of individual naming defeats information conveyed by a recognized group label.

moves.speaker: Paulogia
moves.claim: First Corinthians 15 is an early creed, but Paul learned it rather than witnessing the reported group appearances himself.
moves.warrant: Paulogia immediately retracts his nursery-rhyme label, substitutes creed, and distinguishes an early received formula from first-person reports by most apostles.
moves.inference: Early transmission does not itself establish firsthand testimony from every person included in the grouped claim.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This complete Paulogia turn preserves the immediate retraction, the earliness concession, and the source-dependence objection before McDowell responds.
moves.attributionRationale: The correction and resulting source distinction are explicit and continuous.
moves.importanceRationale: It accepts earliness while maintaining the central firsthand-evidence objection.

burdenContact.rationale: It separates an early received group report from each apostle’s own testimony.

responseComponents.description: Concedes the early group formula but disputes the premise that it functions like direct testimony from all grouped individuals.

moves.speaker: Sean McDowell
moves.claim: A historian can test whether a claim is multiply attested across genres and books without assuming all of Acts, John, or the Gospels are true.
moves.warrant: McDowell points to Peter’s preaching in Acts, the First Corinthians 15 group reference, the Gospels, and early sources as distinct attestations.
moves.inference: The conclusion that apostles believed they experienced the risen Jesus does not require wholesale acceptance of scripture or direct authorship by every apostle.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: McDowell’s full clarification begins with his historical method and ends with the limited conclusion about experiences believed to be of the risen Jesus.
moves.attributionRationale: The methodological clarification is clear; garbled phrases in listing sources are not treated as exact propositions.
moves.importanceRationale: It directly answers the source-dependence objection with a multiple-attestation method.

burdenContact.rationale: It offers a source-critical route to the group-belief conclusion.

responseComponents.description: Answers the premise that indirect receipt prevents the group claim from gaining support across independent genres and sources.

moves.speaker: Paulogia
moves.claim: Peter and Paul probably died and were sincere, but most other apostolic death traditions are inconclusive or weaker than McDowell’s classifications.
moves.warrant: Late, embellished, or apocryphal traditions do not match the strongest extrabiblical cases.
moves.inference: Secure death evidence is too narrow for a broad apostolic martyrdom argument.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The passage covers the graded traditions, strongest accepted cases, and explicit Peter-Paul concession.
moves.attributionRationale: The overall concession is clear, but captions confuse James identities and category labels.
moves.audioVerificationReason: Verify named James figures and precise probability labels before adjudication.
moves.importanceRationale: It concedes the strongest cases while limiting extension.

burdenContact.rationale: It narrows historically supported deaths to accepted cases.

moves.speaker: Sean McDowell
moves.claim: The traditions should be graded rather than treated as an all-twelve claim; strong central cases retain force while others remain weaker or inconclusive.
moves.warrant: McDowell distinguishes probability levels and emphasizes Peter and Paul as central founders whose conduct bears on sincere belief.
moves.inference: The argument does not depend on every traditional death.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The passage includes McDowell’s corrections, inconclusive group, and consequence from central figures.
moves.attributionRationale: The grading and central-figures inference are clear, but names and labels are partially garbled.
moves.audioVerificationReason: Verify named-person probability assignments before adjudication.
moves.importanceRationale: This states the actual scope of the death evidence.

burdenContact.rationale: It identifies why the strongest individual cases matter.

responseComponents.description: Accepts graded uncertainty but disputes that limiting the secure deaths defeats the central-figure case.

moves.speaker: Paulogia
moves.claim: Peter and Paul may sincerely have reached resurrection belief through different individual paths without a group resurrection event.
moves.warrant: Paulogia sketches Peter as an early believer and Paul as a later visionary convert, leaving only two sincere people to explain on his assessment.
moves.inference: No unusual collective explanation is required if the secure pool is two individuals.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The passage states the two-person hypothesis, distinct pathways, and explanatory consequence.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: we just have to explain how two people came to sincerely believe something
moves.attributionRationale: The structure is clear, but wording about Paul’s guilt and vision details is uncertain.
moves.audioVerificationReason: Verify the causal proposal about Paul and treat it as a hypothesis.
moves.importanceRationale: This is con’s principal alternative explanation.

burdenContact.rationale: It scales a naturalistic explanation to the accepted evidence.

responseComponents.description: Accepts two central sincere figures and argues that individual pathways explain them without a group event.

moves.speaker: Sean McDowell
moves.claim: Even the minimal concession of Peter and Paul is significant because two central spokespeople from different backgrounds risked their lives for the same belief.
moves.warrant: Peter followed Jesus as one of the twelve, while Paul had persecuted the movement before becoming a teacher and writer.
moves.inference: The two accepted cases are not evidentially negligible.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The passage directly answers the two-person hypothesis and closes after the shared costly-belief inference.
moves.attributionRationale: The Peter-Paul contrast and limited inference are explicit.
moves.importanceRationale: It preserves motion relevance under con’s narrow minimum.

burdenContact.rationale: It argues that two central costly witnesses add sincerity evidence.

responseComponents.description: Answers that the two accepted figures remain independently significant because of their different origins and shared costly belief.

moves.audioVerificationReason: Verify any material reliance on exact witness-population figures or named writings; assess the broader resistance and investigability claim only from clear wording.
moves.speaker: Sean McDowell
moves.claim: The movement’s early resurrection message faced Jewish and Roman resistance and arose while many people connected to Jesus’s life could still investigate it.
moves.warrant: McDowell argues that proclaiming Jesus over Caesar carried cultural cost and that surviving witnesses and other writings remained available during the movement’s growth.
moves.inference: Explaining only Peter and Paul does not, on his view, explain the broader origin and expansion of the church.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This distinct McDowell passage follows the two-witness point and develops cultural resistance, living investigation, and the church-origin inference before Paulogia responds.
moves.attributionRationale: The inferential line is clear, but the captions garble specific population numbers and some document names.
moves.importanceRationale: It broadens the pro answer from two individuals to public movement formation.

burdenContact.rationale: It connects wider public context and available witnesses to group-level corroboration.

moves.audioVerificationReason: Verify any exact dating or numerical comparison; the anonymous-witness problem is clear.
moves.speaker: Paulogia
moves.claim: Religious claims can grow despite being false and theoretically checkable, while unnamed witnesses from decades earlier are difficult to locate and test.
moves.warrant: Paulogia compares the five-hundred claim to trying to find unnamed attendees of an old local event and notes that later social identification can expand claimed participation.
moves.inference: Contemporary survival and a public group claim do not by themselves make the resurrection report practically falsifiable or historically strong.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: Paulogia’s continuous answer begins with the general legend-growth objection and ends after the practical and social-memory problems with locating the five hundred.
moves.attributionRationale: The checkability objection is clear, but one dating fragment and comparative details are garbled.
moves.importanceRationale: This is con’s direct answer to living-witness investigability and church growth.

burdenContact.rationale: It permits legendary development despite nominal public checkability.

responseComponents.description: Challenges the premises that surviving contemporaries made the claim practically checkable and that growth under those conditions strongly resists legend.

moves.speaker: Sean McDowell
moves.claim: Social networks can locate people, and Paul presented the five-hundred claim early and publicly in a way McDowell reads as inviting investigation.
moves.warrant: He gives a modern chain-of-acquaintance example and emphasizes the timing and public form of First Corinthians 15.
moves.inference: The unnamed group claim is not automatically insulated from contemporary scrutiny, though McDowell says his case does not rest on it.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: McDowell’s complete answer includes the network analogy, application to the five hundred, and explicit limitation before he shifts to methodology.
moves.attributionRationale: The answer and its limiting qualification are explicit; uncertain numbers are not needed.
moves.importanceRationale: It directly answers the practical checkability objection while limiting the point.

burdenContact.rationale: It defends possible contemporary checking of an early group claim.

responseComponents.description: Answers the premise that unnamed witnesses were practically unreachable and notes that this subsidiary claim is not foundational to his case.

moves.speaker: Sean McDowell
moves.claim: McDowell argues that Paulogia’s stated response to a personal appearance sets the evidential requirement unusually high compared with ordinary historical scholarship.
moves.warrant: He quotes Paulogia as saying he would first question his mental faculties even if Jesus appeared and connects that standard to their different historical conclusions.
moves.inference: Methodological skepticism, rather than only a deficiency in the apostolic evidence, explains part of their disagreement.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This complete McDowell move begins when he shifts from the five hundred to methodology and ends after he balances hyper-skepticism against Christian overstatement.
moves.attributionRationale: McDowell clearly introduces and applies the methodological challenge; the quoted wording is contextualized in the following reply.
moves.importanceRationale: It directly contests the evidential standard governing the source dispute.

burdenContact.rationale: It argues that the con-side threshold discounts historically usable evidence.

responseComponents.description: Attributes the very low weight given to early public claims partly to an unusually demanding standard of acceptance.

moves.speaker: Paulogia
moves.claim: Considering imagination, fatigue, or other mental factors alongside the possibility that an appearance is real is reasonable rather than hyper-skeptical.
moves.warrant: Paulogia asks whether McDowell would likewise place both ordinary error and a real appearance on the table when someone reports seeing Jesus.
moves.inference: His historical standard is comparative evaluation of possible explanations, not an unconditional refusal of miracle evidence.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: Paulogia’s full defense begins with clarification of documents he accepts and ends with the completed two-options example before McDowell concedes the point.
moves.attributionRationale: The hypothetical and its qualification are clear; garbled autobiographical asides are not used.
moves.importanceRationale: It answers the methodological characterization and clarifies con’s standard.

burdenContact.rationale: It explains why ordinary-error checks remain live even for sincere reports.

responseComponents.description: Rejects the premise that first checking mental and situational causes amounts to an evidential standard that no appearance could meet.

moves.speaker: Sean McDowell
moves.claim: Initial skepticism toward miracle reports is fair, but persistence under real cost supports that the claimant sincerely believes the report.
moves.warrant: McDowell separates whether history proves a miracle from what costly public commitment reveals about belief.
moves.inference: Suffering supports sincerity while leaving truth as a separate question.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The passage preserves McDowell’s concession to initial skepticism, costly-proclamation example, and explicit limitation to sincerity, ending before the excluded break chain.

selectionBalanceAudit.rationale: Historical standards and checkability contains four pro moves and two con moves because the retained sequence includes McDowell’s distinct cultural-resistance argument, five-hundred checkability reply, methodological-threshold challenge, and later sincerity clarification. Paulogia’s two selected moves each carry broader paired answers: legend growth plus practical checkability, and his defense of ordinary mental-state checks. The 4–2 difference records the source’s asymmetric sequence rather than manufactured symmetry; all other sections remain closer.
